summary: This diff adds a new file, resources/good-adversarial-review.md, a research document defining what makes a good adversarial review (red team/safety evaluation) of AI chatbots. It argues quality comes from discipline, not clever jailbreaks: explicit impact-anchored scope, diverse and partly independent teams, taxonomy-anchored reproducible methodology, manual plus automated testing, severity grading, and a closed remediation-retest loop run continuously. It synthesizes NIST, OWASP, MITRE ATLAS, and lab practices (Microsoft, OpenAI, Anthropic, DeepMind), lists common pitfalls of weak reviews, gives a four-stage recommendation, and closes with caveats about field immaturity, metric fragility, and reliance on vendor sources.

claims.text: NIST AI 600-1 (July 2024) defines 12 GenAI risk categories and organizes red teaming under Measure as a recurring activity.
claims.anchor: ### Scope, threat model, and success criteria

claims.text: Microsoft's Crescendomation achieves 29-61% higher performance on GPT-4 and 49-71% on Gemini-Pro vs other jailbreak techniques, with 98% binary success on GPT-4 (arXiv:2404.01833, USENIX Security 2025).

Anthropic's first-generation Constitutional Classifiers cut jailbreak success rate from an 86% baseline to 4.4% on 10,000 synthetic prompts against Claude 3.5 Sonnet, at a 23.7% compute-cost increase and 0.38% rise in refusals.
claims.anchor: ### Closed remediation loop and continuous testing

claims.text: The HackerOne bug-bounty program invited 405 participants (from ~800 applicants), and a February 2025 public challenge drew 339 participants and over 300,000 interactions across 8 CBRN difficulty levels.
claims.anchor: ### Closed remediation loop and continuous testing

claims.text: 'Constitutional Classifiers++', released January 9, 2026, achieved similar robustness to the original at just ~1% additional compute cost, with no universal jailbreak found after further red-teaming.
claims.anchor: ### Closed remediation loop and continuous testing

claims.text: OpenAI's external red-teaming white paper (arXiv 2503.16431, 2025) lays out four design steps for a red-teaming campaign and four campaign goals.

risks.anchor: ### Closed remediation loop and continuous testing
risks.note: The 'Constitutional Classifiers++' figures (Jan 9, 2026 release, ~1% additional compute cost) carry no primary-source citation (no arXiv/paper link), unlike the first-generation classifier stats in the same paragraph, which do cite a HackerOne program with concrete counts.

The document itself flags that some figures come from vendor blogs and secondary write-ups rather than primary papers, and says rapidly evolving 2026 items (e.g., NIST CAISI agent initiatives, ATLAS version counts) should be reverified before operational use.

least_confident: Whether the 'Constitutional Classifiers++' claim (January 9, 2026 release, ~1% additional compute cost, no universal jailbreak found) is accurate, since the chunk gives no citation for it and elsewhere labels similar forward-looking items as unverified/evolving.
